explanation: std::vector is a fundamental container in the C++ Standard Library that provides a dynamic array, allowing for automatic resizing and safe memory management. This concept promotes best practices by replacing raw arrays, which can lead to common pitfalls like buffer overflows, memory leaks, or undefined behavior from manual memory handling. In real-world scenarios, such as processing user inputs, storing data from files, or building algorithms, std::vector is preferred for its efficiency, ease of use, and safety features like bounds checking. Idiomatic C++ code emphasizes using std::vector over C-style arrays to write cleaner, more maintainable code that adheres to modern C++ standards.
syntax:
std::vector<T> vec;  // Declares an empty vector of type T (e.g., int, std::string)
vec.push_back(element);  // Adds an element to the end, automatically resizing if needed
vec.size();  // Returns the current number of elements
vec.at(index);  // Accesses an element with bounds checking to avoid out-of-bounds errors (best practice over [] operator for safety)
vec.clear();  // Removes all elements, useful for reusing the vector in loops or functions
code_example: std::vector<int> numbers;  // Create an empty vector of integers
// Iterate using a range-based for loop (idiomatic C++ for readability)
std::cout << num << std::endl;  // Output each element
// Demonstrate safe access with bounds checking
std::cout << "Accessing second element: " << numbers.at(1) << std::endl;  // Safe access
example_explanation: This code example illustrates a real-world usage scenario, such as collecting and processing a list of numbers in a program that handles variable input sizes, like reading from a file or user interface. By using std::vector, we avoid common pitfalls: push_back() handles dynamic growth without manual resizing, and at() provides bounds checking to prevent crashes from invalid indices, unlike the unsafe [] operator. Best practices here include using range-based for loops for idiomatic and error-free iteration, checking for emptiness before access, and leveraging automatic memory management to eliminate leaks. In practice, this pattern enhances code reliability and maintainability in applications like data processing or game development.
